1.title: Bring Your Own Cloud to Replit
1.author: The Replit Team
1.description:
Enterprise teams want to build apps connected to their company’s systems and data. But strict security requirements often mean development and production must stay within the isolation and control of their own cloud.



Replit has steadily expanded its governance and isolation posture with many governance tools, separate development and production databases and a single-tenant Replit offering for enterprises.



Now, we’re introducing Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) for Replit, with options for development and production in your cloud, whether you use Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, or Amazon Web Services. Our approach gives security and platform teams greater isolation and control while preserving the familiar Replit experience.

5.title: UI Trends That Are Actually Happening, Part 2: What Changed Since Spring (And Why Users Now Want a…
5.author: Mohit Phogat
5.description:
UI Trends That Are Actually Happening, Part 2: What Changed Since Spring (And Why Users Now Want a Dial)

Six months later, some trends held, some reversed, and users got more say over how interfaces look.

Six months ago, I wrote about eight UI trends that were showing up in real products, not just design portfolios. The argument was pretty simple: a trend is worth paying attention to when it changes how people actually use software.

Well, it’s October now. And some of those trends have developed in ways I didn’t entirely expect.

Apple, a company famous for making design decisions on everyone’s behalf, is now giving people a slider to adjust its interface. Google is experimenting with generating entire interfaces instead of just answering questions. Design tools can turn a rough idea into something surprisingly close to a working prototype.

Meanwhile, design tokens have been quietly doing the unglamorous work of making all these things easier to build and maintain.

Not every prediction aged equally well. Some needed qualifications, others have become more relevant, and a few are still waiting for the evidence to catch up with the excitement.

So this isn’t another list of shiny things to copy into your next project.

It’s a follow-up to Part 1: UI Trends That Are Actually Happening (and Worth Paying Attention To), with four developments worth revisiting, what actually changed, and what I’d take from them as someone working with both design files and frontend code.

1. Users Get a Dial

Apple’s Liquid Glass is probably one of the better examples of a design trend meeting reality.

When iOS 26 introduced the new visual language, the idea sounded reasonable enough. Translucent surfaces, fluid transitions, controls that adapt to their surroundings. Everything looking a little more connected.

And visually, it could look great.

Using it was another matter.

In October 2025, Nielsen Norman Group published a critique of Liquid Glass, pointing out how transparency over busy backgrounds could obscure content rather than help people focus on it.

The review also raised concerns about crowded tap targets, changing control positions, and navigation patterns that made familiar actions harder to find.

That last part matters more than it sounds.

People build habits around interfaces. They remember where buttons are, how menus behave, and what happens when they tap something. If those things keep moving, the interface stops feeling familiar.

And no, making the animation smoother doesn’t solve that.

There’s an older Nielsen Norman Group study that puts the discoverability problem into perspective. In 2016 research on hidden navigation, the researchers found that hiding a website’s main navigation reduced discoverability almost in half.

That study wasn’t about Liquid Glass, and it shouldn’t be treated as a direct measurement of Apple’s design. But it illustrates why hiding or obscuring important controls deserves scrutiny.

Now here’s the interesting part.

With iOS 27, released in September 2026, Apple introduced a slider that lets users adjust Liquid Glass from ultra-clear to fully tinted.

Instead of choosing between fixed appearances, users can adjust how transparent the interface feels. Apple also describes improvements to contrast and readability in the update. Source: Apple, September 2026.

It’s not an option to remove Liquid Glass entirely, but it is more control than users had before.

I find this particularly interesting because it connects to trend #8 from Part 1: personalization that doesn’t overreach.

Back then, I argued that personalization works better when it adapts an interface without making the entire experience unpredictable.

Apple’s slider is a good example of that distinction. The navigation and basic structure stay familiar. Users simply get more say in how the interface looks.

What this means for designers and developers: Don’t make people choose between your visual style and their ability to use the product.

Test controls over real backgrounds. Check contrast with actual content, not just the beautiful placeholder image in the design file. Keep important actions visible and tap targets comfortable.

And when appearance is genuinely subjective, consider giving users a choice.

A settings slider won’t rescue a fundamentally confusing interface. But at least it admits that one visual treatment doesn’t work equally well for everyone.

Turns out the future of glassmorphism involves letting people decide how much glass they want.

Fair enough.

2. Generative UI Is Interesting. But Not Everything Needs to Generate Itself.

In Part 1, I talked about AI working as a layer inside products rather than appearing as another feature asking for attention.

Generative UI takes that idea somewhere slightly different.

Instead of fitting generated content into an existing interface, the system creates an interface specifically for the user’s request.

Say you’re comparing two home loans.

A traditional assistant might explain interest rates and repayment calculations in several paragraphs. A generative interface could produce a calculator with adjustable values, a comparison chart, and a payment breakdown.

Same information, but something you can actually interact with.

Google explored this in research published on November 18, 2025. Its generative UI study compared different ways of presenting responses, including professionally created websites, generated interfaces, text, and Markdown.

The results were interesting.

Expert-made websites received the highest preference rates, with generative UI close behind. Both were preferred substantially more than conventional text-based responses.

There is, however, an important detail: the evaluation didn’t account for generation time.

Google acknowledged that its implementation could sometimes take a minute or more to generate an interface, and that outputs occasionally contained inaccuracies.

A minute might be acceptable when you’re exploring a complicated topic. It’s considerably less acceptable when you’re trying to check an order status or update a customer’s address.

And an incorrect generated chart isn’t better than correct plain text just because it has rounded corners.

There’s another problem worth considering: consistency.

Think about applications people open several times every day. Accounting software, inventory systems, CRM dashboards, project management tools.

People learn those interfaces.

They remember where the filters are. They know which column contains the information they need. They develop shortcuts without consciously thinking about them.

If the system generates a significantly different layout every time, that familiarity disappears.

My take: Generative UI is better suited to one-off tasks, explanations, and exploratory questions than to replacing everyday application interfaces.

A generated interactive explanation of how a mortgage works? Great.

A reporting tool that creates a custom chart for an unusual question? Also useful.

An invoice dashboard that rearranges itself every Monday? Please, we already have enough problems on Mondays.

The more practical direction is probably a combination of both approaches: a stable product interface with generated views where they genuinely make a task easier.

For developers, this also introduces a new responsibility.

Generated interfaces still need reliable data, accessible controls, clear error states, and boundaries around what users can do. A generated financial calculator, for example, should not invent values or silently change assumptions.

We might be able to generate the interface on demand. We don’t get to generate trust quite so easily.

3. Prompt-to-Prototype Tools Are Getting Better at the Messy Parts

The first wave of prompt-based design tools was impressive for about thirty seconds.

You typed something like “create a modern SaaS dashboard,” and received a polished collection of cards, charts, gradients, and suspiciously perfect spacing.

Great screenshot.

Then you asked it to handle a long company name, a validation error, or a table with fifty records.

Suddenly, things became less impressive.

The interesting development in 2026 isn’t that tools can generate a screen. It’s that they’re becoming more useful during the actual design process.

Google’s Stitch is a good example.

In March 2026, Google introduced a major Stitch update, moving the tool towards a broader design canvas where users could explore and refine interfaces using prompts, images, text, and code.

Then, in May, Google announced real-time design capabilities, allowing users to watch the tool work and steer iterations while they were being generated.

That’s a more meaningful development than producing another dashboard from a single prompt.

Because real design work doesn’t happen in a single prompt.

Requirements change. A client wants another filter. The mobile version needs a different arrangement. A form that seemed straightforward suddenly needs conditional fields.

And somewhere between all of that, someone decides the primary button should be a slightly different shade of blue.

We’ve all been there.

But it’s worth separating faster design work from better design work.

An older Figma survey offers a useful reality check. In January 2025, Figma surveyed 2,500 designers and developers globally. According to TechRadar’s report on the findings, 78% said AI made their workflows more efficient, but only 58% believed it improved the quality of their work.

Those numbers are over a year old, not fresh October 2026 results. They also cover AI tools broadly, not Stitch specifically.

Still, the gap between efficiency and quality is worth remembering.

Producing five screens in ten minutes is useful. Discovering that none of them handles an actual user’s problem is less useful.

One experiment I’d like to run at Flux8Labs is taking an existing product screen and recreating it using Stitch.

Not a fictional startup landing page. Something with actual requirements.

A vendor registration form or product-management dashboard would work well.

I’d compare the original and generated versions using the same content and tasks. Which one handles validation better? What happens with long text? Are the empty states understandable? Can someone navigate it with a keyboard? Does it work on a smaller phone?

I’d also compare the time needed to build and refine both versions.

That’s where the value of a tool becomes easier to judge.

The question for design teams isn’t whether these tools can generate attractive screens anymore.

It’s whether they can reduce the work between an initial idea and a usable, maintainable product.

And for developers, there’s another test: what happens after the design is exported?

Generated code still needs to fit the application’s component structure, data handling, accessibility rules, and responsive behaviour.

A prototype isn’t production-ready just because it runs in a browser.

That particular distinction has saved me from a few headaches.

4. Design Systems Are Becoming Easier for Tools to Understand

This is probably the least visually exciting trend on the list.

Which, naturally, makes it one of the more useful ones.

In Part 1, I mentioned how design tokens were becoming a bigger part of design-system workflows.

The development worth revisiting is standardisation.

On October 28, 2025, the W3C Design Tokens Community Group published the first stable Design Tokens specification.

The specification, version 2025.10, provides a common format for describing things such as colours, spacing, typography, and other design decisions.

It also supports token relationships, themes, modern colour formats, and workflows across multiple platforms.

To be precise, this is a stable Community Group specification, not a formal W3C Recommendation.

Why does that matter?

Because design systems have a long-standing problem: the same design decision often exists in several places.

A colour lives in Figma. Another copy exists in a CSS file. A mobile developer has a separate version. Someone changes the brand colour, and suddenly half the product is updated while the other half looks like it missed the meeting.

Design tokens provide a way to define those decisions consistently.

Instead of hardcoding the same hexadecimal colour in twenty components, a team can refer to a semantic token such as color.action.primary.

Change the value in the right place, and the components using it can inherit the update.

The idea isn’t new. What’s important is making it easier for different tools to understand the same token data.

There’s evidence that design-system teams were already moving in this direction.

The zeroheight Design Systems Report 2025, based on 294 survey respondents with data collected between September and November 2024, found that 84% reported including design tokens in their design systems, compared with 56% in the previous report.

That’s a finding about the surveyed teams, not a claim that 84% of every product team in the industry uses tokens.

Another useful development arrived in April 2026, when Google open-sourced the draft DESIGN.md specification.

The idea is to make design-system rules and intent easier to exchange between tools, including Stitch.

It’s not a replacement for the Design Tokens specification. Tokens describe structured design values; DESIGN.md attempts to communicate broader design guidance and reasoning.

But the direction is interesting.

Instead of repeatedly explaining that a particular colour is reserved for destructive actions, or that a certain component should follow specific spacing rules, teams can make more of that information available to the tools producing interfaces.

Of course, there’s a catch.

Standardised tokens don’t automatically create a good design system.

You still need sensible names, documented components, clear ownership, accessibility checks, and a process for handling changes without breaking half the application.

If your team has four different primary buttons, exporting their styles into a standardised file doesn’t solve the underlying problem.

Congratulations. You now have four inconsistent buttons in a more portable format.

For designers and developers, the real opportunity is reducing the translation work between design and code.

The less time spent copying values, correcting mismatched spacing, and recreating components, the more time there is to deal with the parts that actually require judgement.

And those parts are not going away.

The Common Thread

Looking back at the original eight trends, I don’t think the broad direction has changed that much.

What has changed is how the industry is dealing with the consequences.

Liquid Glass is still here, but Apple is giving users more control over it.

Generated interfaces are getting more capable, but the research also makes their limitations harder to ignore.

Prompt-based design tools are moving beyond producing attractive first drafts towards supporting ongoing iteration.

And design systems are getting better at carrying consistent decisions between tools rather than relying on someone to copy values manually.

None of these developments means designers or developers can stop thinking about the fundamentals.

People still need readable text, predictable navigation, understandable feedback, and interfaces that work when the data isn’t perfect.

A product still needs sensible defaults. Forms still need useful error messages. Loading states need to communicate what’s happening. Important actions shouldn’t disappear just because someone wanted a cleaner layout.

These are fairly ordinary concerns.

They’re also the ones that tend to become painfully obvious after a product reaches real users.

For me, the more interesting shift is that flexibility is becoming valuable, but only when it doesn’t come at the expense of predictability.

Users should be able to adjust an interface without having to relearn it.

Designers should be able to explore ideas faster without treating generated output as finished work.

Developers should be able to move design decisions between tools without manually rebuilding everything.

And product teams should measure whether any of this actually helps people complete tasks.

Not every trend needs to appear in every product.

An internal inventory dashboard doesn’t need the visual drama of a music app. A one-time interactive explanation doesn’t need the same rigid layout as accounting software. And a small website doesn’t automatically need an elaborate token pipeline.

The right decision still depends on what you’re building, who uses it, and what problem you’re trying to solve.

Six months ago, the question was which trends were actually happening.

Now I think the more useful question is which ones are making products better.

Because getting an interface to look impressive is only part of the job.

Getting it to behave properly, especially when nobody’s watching, is the harder part.

And if your users need a tutorial to find the settings button, maybe hold off on adding another animation.

If you read Part 1, which of those trends do you think has aged the best? I’m particularly interested in what designers and developers are seeing in actual projects, not just demos.

I write about UI, UX, frontend development, and the decisions behind building products people can actually use.
